subject: Biotechnology
title: Transgenic Crops
description: A quick, practical guide to Transgenic Crops.

hook.text: The Flavr Savr tomato hit shelves in 1994 — the first GMO food approved for sale. It flopped commercially.

buildup.text: An antisense gene slowed the enzyme that softens tomatoes — extending shelf life by weeks.

discovery.text: Today's transgenic crops are far more successful — Bt corn, herbicide-tolerant soy, and virus-resistant papaya.

twist.text: Europe mostly bans GMO cultivation — while the Americas, China, and India plant billions of acres.

climax.text: Arctic apples do not brown when sliced — gene silencing removed the browning enzyme without adding foreign DNA.

punchline.text: Transgenic crops feed billions — the science works, the debate continues.

quiz.question: Why was the Flavr Savr tomato a commercial failure despite being scientifically sound?
options: It was toxic and recalled by the FDA
It had poor flavor and high production costs despite extended shelf life
It was banned in all countries before it could reach consumers

details.summary: Transgenic crops contain genes from other species introduced through genetic engineering to confer traits like insect resistance, herbicide tolerance, or enhanced nutrition. Bt crops producing bacterial insecticidal proteins and Roundup Ready soybeans are the most widely planted examples.

faq.question: How do Bt crops protect themselves from insects?
faq.answer: Bt crops express Cry proteins from Bacillus thuringiensis bacteria. These proteins are specifically toxic to certain insect larvae when ingested but harmless to mammals, birds, and most beneficial insects. The toxin creates pores in the insect gut membrane, causing death within days.

faq.question: Have transgenic crops fulfilled their promise after 25 years?
faq.answer: Meta-analyses show Bt crops reduced insecticide use by 37 percent and increased yields by 22 percent on average. Benefits are largest in developing countries. However, herbicide-resistant weeds have evolved, and corporate seed control remains contentious.
